questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The shop is having a ________ — everything is at half price this week.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) sale
Why: A "sale" is an event at which goods are sold at reduced prices.
Why not the others: (B) A sail is the cloth on a boat. (C) is a verb. (D) is a past form of the verb.
Key point: Sale (noun) is related to sell (verb).

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
She answered every question without the slightest ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) hesitation
Why: After "the slightest", a noun is needed: "without the slightest hesitation".
Why not the others: (A) is a verb. (B) is an adjective. (C) is an adverb.
Key point: Adjective + noun: the slightest hesitation.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "It was only after the match"
A. how badly
B. that the players realised
C. they had been injured
D. during the game
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, A, C, D
Why: "It was only after the match that the players realised (B) how badly (A) they had been injured (C) during the game (D)." "It was ... that" is followed by the main clause, and "how badly" introduces what they realised.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) break the "It was ... that" pattern. (D) separates "how badly" from "they had been injured".
Key point: It was + time + that + clause.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The rocket launch was ________, and the satellite reached its orbit.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) successful
Why: After "was", an adjective is needed: "was successful".
Why not the others: (B) is a noun ("was a success" would need "a"). (C) is an adverb. (D) is a verb.
Key point: Success (noun), succeed (verb), successful (adjective).

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
He talks ________ he knew everything about computers.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) as if
Why: "As if" introduces an imagined or unreal comparison: he talks in the way someone who knew everything would talk.
Why not the others: (A) shows purpose. (B) shows a condition. (C) gives a reason.
Key point: After "as if", the past tense often shows that something is not true.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The cost of the repairs will be ________ by the landlord, not the tenant.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) borne
Why: "Borne" is the past participle of "bear" in the sense of carrying or paying a cost.
Why not the others: (A) "Born" is used only for birth. (C) is a rare old word for a stream or boundary. (D) is the simple past and cannot follow "be".
Key point: A child is born; a cost is borne.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Passive voice, present perfect with someone
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
Someone has stolen my bag.
options: A) My bag was stolen by someone.
C) My bag had been stolen.
D) My bag has been stolen.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) My bag has been stolen.
Why: The present perfect "has stolen" becomes "has been stolen"; a vague agent such as "someone" is usually left out.
Why not the others: (A) changes the tense to the simple past. (B) changes it to the simple present. (C) changes it to the past perfect.
Key point: Drop vague agents such as someone, people and they.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
He said to her, "Why did you come late?"
options: A) He asked her why did she come late.
B) He told her why she came late.
C) He asked her why she had come late.
D) He asked her why had she come late.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) He asked her why she had come late.
Why: A question is reported with "asked"; the simple past "did you come" becomes the past perfect "she had come" in statement order.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) keep question word order. (B) uses "told" and does not shift the tense.
Key point: Simple past → past perfect in reported speech.

questions.question: Choose the one word for: "An abnormal fear of water"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Hydrophobia
Why: Hydrophobia (Greek "hydro", water + "phobos", fear) is a fear of water.
Why not the others: (A) is a fear of closed spaces. (B) is a fear of heights. (D) is a fear or dislike of foreigners.
Key point: "-phobia" means fear; the prefix names its object.

questions.sub_topic: Synonym pairs: assemble, rare, remote, mend
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of synonyms:
A. assemble — gather
B. rare — common
C. remote — distant
D. mend — repair
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, C and D only
C) B, C and D only
D) A, B, C and D
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, C and D only
Why: Assemble and gather, remote and distant, mend and repair have the same meaning.
Why not the others: Pair B is a pair of antonyms. Options (B), (C) and (D) include pair B.
Key point: Test each pair on its own.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Meek
(B) Morose
(C) Lavish
(D) Nimble

List-II
(I) Spending or given in great amounts
(II) Quick and light in movement
(III) Quiet, gentle and easily imposed on
(IV) Gloomy and bad-tempered
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Meek — gentle and submissive (III); morose — sullen and gloomy (IV); lavish — generous in amount, as in a lavish feast (I); nimble — quick and light, as in nimble fingers (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps meek and morose; (B) swaps morose and lavish; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: Meek and morose are both quiet, but only morose is gloomy.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
The firefighters took two hours to ________ the fire in the warehouse.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) put out
Why: "Put out" means to extinguish a fire or light.
Why not the others: (A) means to wear or switch on. (B) means to save money. (D) means to spend time or effort, or to install.
Key point: Fires are put out.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: one of, elder, committee, furniture
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. One of the players was injured.
B. He is elder than me.
C. The committee were divided in their opinions.
D. I have bought a new furnitures.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: B) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A and C only
Why: In A, the subject "one" is singular. In C, the members of the committee are thought of as individuals, so the plural verb is correct.
Why not the others: B should be "older than" ("elder" is not used with "than"). D should be "new furniture" ("furniture" is uncountable). Options (B), (C) and (D) include B or D.
Key point: Collective nouns take a plural verb when the members act separately.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
Keep the wet clothes ________ from the dry ones.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) separate
Why: The correct spelling is s-e-p-a-r-a-t-e.
Why not the others: (A) has "e" in place of the first "a". (B) has "e" in place of the second "a". (C) misses the first "a".
Key point: There is "a rat" in separate.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to ACUMEN:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Shrewdness
Why: Acumen means the ability to make good, quick judgements, especially in business; shrewdness has the same sense.
Why not the others: (A) only looks similar. (B) takes the idea of sharpness literally. (C) Acumen may bring wealth but does not mean it.
Key point: Business acumen is skill in judging business matters.

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to DEFICIENT:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Adequate
Why: Deficient means not having enough of something; adequate means enough.
Why not the others: (B) is a synonym. (C) only sounds similar. (D) means faulty, which is close to deficient.
Key point: A diet deficient in iron does not contain enough iron.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Wear a sweater, or you will ________ a cold.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) catch
Why: The fixed collocation is "catch a cold".
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not go with "a cold" in this sense.
Key point: Catch a cold, catch a train, catch someone's eye.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
You can pay ________ in cash or by UPI.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) either
Why: "Either ... or" offers a choice between two things.
Why not the others: (B) pairs with "nor". (C) pairs with "and". (D) would need "whether ... or not" and does not fit here.
Key point: Either ... or; neither ... nor; both ... and.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
In the ________ heat of May, the roads of Delhi were almost empty at noon.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) scorching
Why: "Scorching" means extremely hot, which explains the empty roads at noon in May.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) suggest comfortable or cold weather.
Key point: The setting (May, noon, empty roads) decides the word.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. does it snow
B. Seldom
C. in the plains of north India
D. even in the coldest winters
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) B, A, C, D
Why: "Seldom (B) does it snow (A) in the plains of north India (C) even in the coldest winters (D)." After "Seldom", the auxiliary comes before the subject.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) start with a lower-case part, so "Seldom" is lost in the middle.
Key point: Seldom/Rarely/Never + auxiliary + subject + verb.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. whose paintings won the prize
B. is only twelve years old
C. The artist
D. at the national exhibition
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C, A, D, B
Why: "The artist (C) whose paintings won the prize (A) at the national exhibition (D) is only twelve years old (B)." The "whose" clause must follow "The artist", and "at the national exhibition" completes "won the prize".
Why not the others: (A) and (C) push the "whose" clause to the end, away from "The artist". (B) starts with a lower-case part.
Key point: A relative clause sits right after the noun it describes.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Arsonist
(B) Egotist
(C) Centenarian
(D) Eavesdropper

List-II
(I) A person who is a hundred years old or more
(II) A person who secretly listens to others' private talk
(III) A person who deliberately sets property on fire
(IV) A person who talks too much about himself or herself
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Arsonist — one who sets fires on purpose (III); egotist — one who talks constantly of himself or herself (IV); centenarian — someone aged a hundred or more (I); eavesdropper — one who listens secretly (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps arsonist and egotist; (B) swaps egotist and centenarian; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: "Cent-" means hundred.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Keep up with
(B) Keep off
(C) Keep on
(D) Keep out

List-II
(I) Continue doing something
(II) Not enter, or stop from entering
(III) Stay at the same level or pace as
(IV) Stay away from or avoid touching
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Keep up with the class — stay at the same pace (III); keep off the grass — stay away from (IV); keep on talking — continue (I); "Keep out!" — do not enter (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (B) swaps the middle two; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: The particle changes the meaning of "keep".

questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Simile
(B) Alliteration
(C) Oxymoron
(D) Climax

List-II
(I) He lost his job, then his house, and at last his hope.
(II) The ice was as cold as a stone in a river.
(III) A cruel kindness made her leave home.
(IV) Five funny frogs fell from the fence.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: "As cold as a stone" — simile (II); repeated "f" sounds — alliteration (IV); "cruel kindness" joins opposites — oxymoron (III); job, house, hope rise in importance — climax (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps simile and alliteration; (C) swaps alliteration and oxymoron; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: In a climax, ideas are arranged in rising order of importance.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
He offered a SINCERE apology for his rude remark.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Genuine
Why: Sincere means honest and meant truly; genuine means the same.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) describe an apology but not whether it is meant.
Key point: A sincere apology is felt, not just said.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
The travellers were EXHAUSTED after the twelve-hour journey.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Refreshed
Why: Exhausted means extremely tired; refreshed means rested and full of energy again.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are unrelated in meaning. (C) is a synonym.
Key point: Exhausted is stronger than tired.

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: wet blanket, face the music, thick and thin, hot potato
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) A wet blanket
(B) To face the music
(C) Through thick and thin
(D) A hot potato

List-II
(I) In good times and bad
(II) A person who spoils others' fun
(III) A controversial issue that people avoid
(IV) To accept the consequences of one's actions
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: A wet blanket — a spoilsport (II); face the music — accept the consequences (IV); through thick and thin — in good and bad times (I); a hot potato — a controversial issue (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Learn idioms as whole units of meaning.

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to BIZARRE:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ordinary
Why: Bizarre means very strange or unusual; ordinary means normal and usual.
Why not the others: (A) is a synonym. (B) only sounds a little like "bazaar". (D) is unrelated.
Key point: Do not confuse bizarre (strange) with bazaar (market).

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
All players must abide ________ the decision of the umpire.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) by
Why: The fixed expression is "abide by", meaning to accept and obey a rule or decision.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not used with "abide" in this sense.
Key point: Abide by the rules.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
He was jealous ________ his brother's new bicycle.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) of
Why: The fixed expression is "jealous of".
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not standard with "jealous".
Key point: Jealous of, envious of.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The taxi driver demanded an ________ fare, three times the usual rate.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) exorbitant
Why: "Exorbitant" means far too high, which fits a fare three times the usual rate.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) all suggest a low or reasonable price.
Key point: "Three times the usual rate" explains the word.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. A butterfly begins life as a tiny egg laid on a leaf.
B. Inside this case, its body is completely rebuilt.
C. The caterpillar that hatches eats steadily and grows fast.
D. When it is fully grown, it forms a hard case called a pupa.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, C, D, B
Why: A begins with the egg; C introduces "The caterpillar that hatches"; D says "When it is fully grown, it forms ... a pupa"; B follows with "Inside this case".
Why not the others: (B) forms the pupa before the caterpillar hatches. (C) begins with "The caterpillar that hatches" before the egg. (D) mentions "this case" before the case is formed.
Key point: "This case" points back to the pupa.

questions.question:
Select the words that mean "extremely dirty and unpleasant":
A. filthy
B. stolid
C. squalid
D. valid
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
D) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A and C only
Why: "Filthy" and "squalid" both mean very dirty and unpleasant.
Why not the others: B (stolid) means calm and showing little emotion. D (valid) means legally or logically acceptable. Options (A), (C) and (D) include one of them.
Key point: Squalid conditions are dirty and neglected.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. out to sea
B. before dawn
C. In Kerala, many fishermen
D. row their boats
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) C, D, A, B
Why: The opener with the subject (C) is followed by the verb and object (D), where they row (A) and when (B).
Why not the others: (A) puts "out to sea" between the subject and the verb. (B) and (D) start with a lower-case part.
Key point: Subject, verb, object, then place and time.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The tailor will ________ the length of the trousers by tomorrow.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) alter
Why: After "will", the base form of a verb is needed; "alter" means to change.
Why not the others: (A) An altar is a holy table in a place of worship. (B) is a noun. (D) is a past form and cannot follow "will".
Key point: Alter (change) and altar (holy table) sound the same.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

India is one of the sunniest large countries in the world. Most regions receive bright sunshine on around three hundred days a year, and the sunlight that falls on the country in a single day carries far more energy than India uses in that time. For millions of villagers, this sunshine is beginning to light homes, run pumps and power small businesses.

Solar panels are made of photovoltaic cells, thin layers of material, usually silicon, that produce electricity when sunlight falls on them. They have no moving parts, make no noise and give off no smoke. Once installed, they need little more than regular cleaning to remove dust.

For a farmer, the most important use of solar power is often the irrigation pump. Many farmers have depended on pumps that run on diesel, which is expensive and must be carried to the field, or on grid electricity, which in some villages comes for only a few hours, often at night. A solar pump works in daylight, when the farmer is in the field, and costs almost nothing to run. Government schemes such as PM-KUSUM, launched in 2019, help farmers meet part of the cost of installing one.

Solar power has its difficulties too. The upfront cost of panels and batteries can be high for a poor household, even though the fuel, sunlight, is free. Batteries are needed to store electricity for the night, and they wear out after some years. Panels must be maintained, and a mini-grid needs trained local mechanics. Yet as prices fall and skills spread, more villages are discovering that the sun overhead is a power station that never sends a bill.

Question: According to the passage, on about how many days a year do most regions of India receive bright sunshine?
options: D) Almost every day of the year
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About three hundred
Why: "Most regions receive bright sunshine on around three hundred days a year."
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are not stated. (D) exaggerates the passage.
Key point: Detail questions are answered from the exact line.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Yet as prices fall and skills spread, more villages are discovering that the sun overhead is a power station that never sends a bill.

Question: Why, according to the passage, is a solar pump especially useful to a farmer?
options: A) It works at night when grid electricity is available
B) It needs diesel only once a month
C) It can be moved easily from village to village
D) It works in daylight and costs almost nothing to run
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It works in daylight and costs almost nothing to run
Why: "A solar pump works in daylight, when the farmer is in the field, and costs almost nothing to run."
Why not the others: (A) describes the grid supply the passage criticises. (B) Solar pumps do not use diesel. (C) is not stated.
Key point: Find the sentence that answers "why" directly.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Yet as prices fall and skills spread, more villages are discovering that the sun overhead is a power station that never sends a bill.

Question: In the last paragraph, "the upfront cost" of solar power means:
options: A) The money paid at the start to buy and install it
B) The daily cost of the sunlight that the panels use
C) The money a family saves by not buying diesel
D) The cost of repairing old panels after many years
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The money paid at the start to buy and install it
Why: The sentence contrasts the high "upfront cost of panels and batteries" with the free fuel: it is the cost paid in advance.
Why not the others: (B) Sunlight is free. (C) is a saving, not a cost. (D) is a later cost, not an upfront one.
Key point: "Up front" means at the beginning, in advance.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Yet as prices fall and skills spread, more villages are discovering that the sun overhead is a power station that never sends a bill.

Question: What can be inferred from the passage about a solar home without a battery?
options: A) It would have no electricity during the day
B) It would need diesel to run its panels
C) It would have little or no solar power at night
D) It would never need any maintenance at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It would have little or no solar power at night
Why: The passage says "Batteries are needed to store electricity for the night"; without them, solar power is available only while the sun shines.
Why not the others: (A) Panels work in daylight. (B) Panels do not use diesel. (D) The passage says panels need cleaning and maintenance.
Key point: Inference follows from a stated fact without adding new ones.

questions.sub_topic: The sun as a power station with no bill
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

India is one of the sunniest large countries in the world. Most regions receive bright sunshine on around three hundred days a year, and the sunlight that falls on the country in a single day carries far more energy than India uses in that time. For millions of villagers, this sunshine is beginning to light homes, run pumps and power small businesses.

Solar panels are made of photovoltaic cells, thin layers of material, usually silicon, that produce electricity when sunlight falls on them. They have no moving parts, make no noise and give off no smoke. Once installed, they need little more than regular cleaning to remove dust.

For a farmer, the most important use of solar power is often the irrigation pump. Many farmers have depended on pumps that run on diesel, which is expensive and must be carried to the field, or on grid electricity, which in some villages comes for only a few hours, often at night. A solar pump works in daylight, when the farmer is in the field, and costs almost nothing to run. Government schemes such as PM-KUSUM, launched in 2019, help farmers meet part of the cost of installing one.

Solar power has its difficulties too. The upfront cost of panels and batteries can be high for a poor household, even though the fuel, sunlight, is free. Batteries are needed to store electricity for the night, and they wear out after some years. Panels must be maintained, and a mini-grid needs trained local mechanics. Yet as prices fall and skills spread, more villages are discovering that the sun overhead is a power station that never sends a bill.

Question: "The sun overhead is a power station that never sends a bill." What does the writer mean?
options: A) Solar companies do not charge villagers anything at all
B) Once installed, solar power uses a free source of energy
C) The government pays every villager's electricity bill
D) Power stations are being built in the sky
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Once installed, solar power uses a free source of energy
Why: The sun supplies energy free of charge, though the passage has admitted the upfront and maintenance costs.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are not stated; panels and batteries cost money. (D) reads the metaphor literally.
Key point: A metaphor in a conclusion sums up the writer's view.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Every Sankranti, the sky over Gopal's colony filled with kites: red, yellow, purple, kites with tails and kites with eyes painted on them. Gopal watched them from the roof of the one-room house where he lived with his father, who drove an auto-rickshaw and believed that kites were a waste of money.

"Twenty rupees for a piece of paper that flies away," his father said. "You can eat for two days on twenty rupees."

So that year Gopal made his own. He cut two thin sticks from an old broom, tied them in a cross with his mother's sewing thread and stretched over them a page from the newspaper his father brought home. He glued the edges with boiled rice. For a tail he used a strip of his torn school shirt. When he had finished, the kite looked like a sheet of yesterday's news with a ragged blue ribbon.

The boys on the next roof laughed until they had to hold their stomachs.

But in the afternoon, when the wind came, Gopal's kite rose. It rose past the water tank and the mobile tower, and it went on rising, a small grey square against the blue, long after the boys had lost three bright kites in their battles. It did not cut anyone's string. It simply stayed up, steady and patient, as if it had all the time in the world.

At sunset, Gopal felt a hand on his shoulder. His father had come home early. He watched the kite for a long moment without speaking. Then he held out his hand. "Let me try," he said.

Question: Why did Gopal's father think kites were a waste of money?
options: A) Kites had once damaged his auto-rickshaw
B) He believed flying kites was dangerous on roofs
C) The money could feed the family for two days
D) The colony had banned kite-flying at Sankranti
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The money could feed the family for two days
Why: He says, "Twenty rupees for a piece of paper that flies away ... You can eat for two days on twenty rupees."
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not stated.
Key point: A character's own words give the reason.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: The kite stayed up "steady and patient, as if it had all the time in the world". The figure of speech here is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Personification
Why: A kite cannot be patient or have time; it is given human qualities — personification.
Why not the others: (A) No opposite words are joined. (C) There is no exaggeration meant to be taken as such. (D) No sound is repeated at the start of words.
Key point: Human qualities given to objects signal personification.

Question: At the end, Gopal's father says, "Let me try." What does this suggest?
options: A) He wants to take the kite away from Gopal
B) He plans to sell the kite to the boys next door
C) He has softened and shares his son's joy
D) He is checking whether the string is strong
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) He has softened and shares his son's joy
Why: He had called kites a waste of money; now, after watching quietly, he asks to fly one himself, showing that his son's kite has won him over.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) do not fit his long, silent watching.
Key point: A final line can show a change of heart.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

They will pull the house down on Monday. The papers have been signed, the furniture sold, and the men with hammers are already measuring the walls with their eyes. For three days it stands empty, like a man who has said goodbye but not yet left the room.

I walk through it one last time. The rooms are larger without the beds and cupboards, and every footstep comes back to me from the bare walls. On the kitchen wall the soot of forty years of cooking has left a dark ghost where the stove used to be. On the door of the store-room, a ladder of pencil lines climbs upwards, each one marked with a name and a year. My own name is near the bottom, beside a line so low that I can hardly believe I was ever that small.

The courtyard is the hardest. The tulsi plant is gone, but its square stone bed is still there, and the neem tree that shaded our afternoon games still drops its yellow leaves on the floor that nobody will sweep again. A sparrow flies in through the broken skylight, looks around as if it, too, is searching for someone, and flies out again.

I close the front door behind me, though there is nothing left inside to keep safe. Habit, I suppose. Or perhaps one wants to leave a house the way one would leave a sleeping person, quietly, without slamming the door on all those years.

Question: "For three days it stands empty, like a man who has said goodbye but not yet left the room." This simile suggests that the house:
options: A) Is crowded with guests who are leaving
B) Is angry with the people who sold it
C) Will be repaired and lived in again
D) Is in a sad, waiting state before its end
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Is in a sad, waiting state before its end
Why: Like someone who has said goodbye but lingers, the empty house waits for its demolition on Monday.
Why not the others: (A) The house is empty. (B) is not suggested. (C) contradicts the first sentence.
Key point: Ask what the two things compared have in common.

Question: What is "the ladder of pencil lines" on the store-room door?
options: A) Marks recording the children's heights over the years
B) A drawing of a ladder by the writer as a child
C) The measurements made by the men with hammers
D) Accounts of household spending kept by the family
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Marks recording the children's heights over the years
Why: Each line is "marked with a name and a year", and the writer's own line is so low that he can hardly believe he "was ever that small".
Why not the others: (B) and (D) do not match "name and a year". (C) The men measure the walls "with their eyes".
Key point: Use the surrounding details to identify what a phrase describes.

Question: "A sparrow flies in ... looks around as if it, too, is searching for someone." The word "too" suggests that:
options: A) Many sparrows have nested in the house for years
B) The sparrow has lost its own nest in the tree
C) The writer also feels he is searching for people who are gone
D) The sparrow is looking for food left by the family
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The writer also feels he is searching for people who are gone
Why: "Too" links the sparrow to the writer: both seem to look for the people and life that once filled the house.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not suggested by "too".
Key point: Small words such as "too" and "also" can carry the meaning of a line.

Question: Why does the writer close the front door, "though there is nothing left inside to keep safe"?
options: A) He is afraid that thieves will steal the furniture
B) Out of habit and respect for the years spent in the house
C) Because the men with hammers have asked him to
D) To stop the sparrow from flying back in
